title: Occupational stress and its association with nurses productivity in the Buea Health District, Cameroon: A cross-sectional study
content:
by Akah Thelma Eni, Kelly Tabe Takang, Odette Dzemo Kibu, Tamoh Clinton Ketum, Tendongfor Nicholas

Background

Occupational stress is a major concern among healthcare workers, particularly nurses, due to its negative impacts on mental health and productivity. Nurses face multiple stressors including heavy workloads, long hours, exposure to infectious diseases, and the emotional toll of patient care. This study assessed the prevalence of occupational stress and its association with nurses’ productivity in the Buea Health District, Cameroon.

Methods

A hospital‑based cross‑sectional study was conducted among 301 nurses using a structured questionnaire to collect socio‑demographic data, occupational stress, and productivity measures. Statistical analysis included descriptive statistics, Chi‑squared tests, and linear regression.

Results

Among the 301 nurses included in the study, 250 (83.1%) were female, and the mean age was 26.3 ± 5.0 years. The prevalence of occupational stress was 46.0% (138/301). Linear regression analysis showed that occupational stress was significantly associated with lower task performance (B = −0.24, 95% CI: −0.29 to −0.18; p < 0.001), lower contextual performance (B = −0.27, 95% CI: −0.36 to −0.18; p < 0.001), and lower overall work productivity (B = −0.56, 95% CI: −0.71 to −0.41; p < 0.001). Occupational stress explained 19.5%, 10.9%, and 15.9% of the variance in task performance, contextual performance, and overall work productivity, respectively. No significant association was observed between occupational stress and counterproductive work behaviour (B = 0.05, 95% CI: −0.04 to 0.14; p = 0.260). Several sociodemographic factors, including sex, marital status, educational level, age, and monthly income, were independently associated with specific dimensions of work productivity.

Conclusion

Occupational stress was associated with reduced task, contextual, and overall work productivity among nurses, but not with counterproductive work behaviour. Interventions aimed at reducing occupational stress may help enhance workforce productivity in healthcare settings.
